units.en: CHAPTER VI. Tonio travels north in comfort and stops in his home town. On a grey afternoon he walks from the smoky station through the narrow streets: everything looks tiny and strangely familiar, as if in a dream. For years he has dreamt that his father scolds him for his wild way of life. He stays at the town's best hotel, in front of which lie the two black stone lions he was afraid of as a child; the staff eye him suspiciously, unable to work out who he is. After a night of confused, longing dreams he wakes to sunshine, dresses with great care and goes out, relieved that nobody recognises him. Almost without knowing it, he lets his feet lead him through the old town.

units.de: Wohin ging er? Ihm war, als stehe die Richtung, die er einschlug, in einem Zusammenhange mit seinen traurigen und seltsam reuevollen Träumen zur Nacht... Auf den Markt ging er, unter den Bogengewölben des Rathauses hindurch, wo Fleischer mit blutigen Händen ihre Ware wogen, auf den Marktplatz, wo hoch, spitzig und vielfach der gotische Brunnen stand. Dort blieb er vor einem Hause stehen, einem schmalen und schlichten, gleich anderen mehr, mit einem geschwungenen, durchbrochenen Giebel, und versank in dessen Anblick. Er las das Namensschild an der Tür und ließ seine Augen ein Weilchen auf jedem der Fenster ruhen. Dann wandte er sich langsam zum Gehen.
units.en: Where was he going? He felt as if the direction he took had something to do with his sad and strangely remorseful dreams of the night... He went to the market, under the arches of the town hall, where butchers with bloody hands were weighing their meat, onto the market square, where the tall, pointed, many-spired Gothic fountain stood. There he stopped in front of a house, a narrow and plain one like many others, with a curved, openwork gable, and became lost in looking at it. He read the name plate on the door and let his eyes rest for a little while on each of the windows. Then he slowly turned to go.
units.explain_en: The words “wo hoch, spitzig und vielfach der gotische Brunnen stand” are exactly the ones used for Inge Holm's home at the start of Chapter II – so we know whose house this is without being told. “Ihm war, als ...” = he felt as if ...: “Mir ist, als hätte ich das schon mal gesehen.” “der Fleischer” = butcher (in southern Germany “der Metzger”). “wiegen” (wog, hat gewogen) = to weigh. “versinken in” = to become absorbed in. “ein Weilchen” = a little while.

units.en: Next Tonio walks out to Hans Hansen's old villa and swings the squeaking garden gate, just as Hans did when they were boys. Then he climbs the steep lane to his parents' house. His heart pounds: he half expects his father to step out of the office and tell him off. But the grand old house has changed. On the landing there is a sign: ‘Volksbibliothek’ – a public library. Inside, poorly dressed clerks sit among long shelves of books. Pretending to be a tourist, Tonio takes out a book and stands at the window. This used to be the breakfast room; there is the bedroom where his grandmother died, and later his father, with Tonio sitting at the foot of the bed and his mother in tears – before she went off with her musician.

units.de: Aber dort hinten, das kleinere, dritte Zimmer, nun ebenfalls ganz mit Büchern angefüllt, die ein dürftiger Mensch bewachte, war lange Jahre hindurch sein eigenes gewesen. Dorthin war er nach der Schule heimgekehrt, nachdem er einen Spaziergang, wie eben jetzt, gemacht, an jener Wand hatte sein Tisch gestanden, in dessen Schublade er seine ersten, innigen und hilflosen Verse verwahrt hatte... Der Walnussbaum... Eine stechende Wehmut durchzuckte ihn. Er blickte seitwärts durchs Fenster hinaus. Der Garten lag wüst, aber der alte Walnussbaum stand an seinem Platze, schwerfällig knarrend und rauschend im Winde.
units.en: But back there, the smaller third room, now also completely filled with books guarded by a shabby-looking man, had been his own for many years. That was where he had come home to after school, after taking a walk just like now; against that wall his desk had stood, in whose drawer he had kept his first heartfelt and helpless poems... The walnut tree... A piercing sadness shot through him. He glanced sideways out of the window. The garden lay neglected, but the old walnut tree still stood in its place, creaking heavily and rustling in the wind.
units.explain_en: The walnut tree, the fountain and the sea were the “friends” of Tonio's youth that he wrote his first poems about. The tree has survived, although everything else has changed. Notice the pluperfect (“war heimgekehrt”, “hatte gestanden”) for the past before the past. “verwahren” = to keep safe (everyday “aufbewahren”). “die Wehmut” = wistful sadness, nostalgia. “wüst” = wild, neglected (compare “die Wüste” = desert). “knarren” = to creak; “rauschen” = to rustle or roar (trees, sea, water).

units.en: Tonio reads a few lines of the book – ‘Yes, that's well done!’ – and leaves. He decides to take the afternoon steamer to Copenhagen. But at the foot of the hotel stairs the owner, Herr Seehaase, and a policeman are waiting for him. The policeman asks for his papers – Tonio has none, only the proofs of a story he is writing. When Tonio gives his name and his profession, the policeman asks whether he is not in fact a wanted man with a complicated, romantic-sounding name, ‘of unknown parents’, who has committed fraud in Munich and is probably fleeing to Denmark. ‘I'm not just claiming that,’ Tonio says nervously. Herr Seehaase says it's only a formality – if the gentleman could just show some kind of document…

units.de: Alle schwiegen. Sollte er der Sache ein Ende machen, indem er sich zu erkennen gab, indem er Herrn Seehaase eröffnete, dass er kein Hochstapler von unbestimmter Zuständigkeit sei, von Geburt kein Zigeuner im grünen Wagen, sondern der Sohn Konsul Krögers, aus der Familie der Kröger? Nein, er hatte keine Lust dazu. Und waren diese Männer der bürgerlichen Ordnung nicht im Grunde ein wenig im Recht? Gewissermaßen war er ganz einverstanden mit ihnen... Er zuckte die Achseln und blieb stumm.
units.en: Everyone was silent. Should he put an end to the matter by revealing who he was, by informing Herr Seehaase that he was not a con man of no fixed abode, not a gypsy in a green caravan by birth, but the son of Consul Kröger, of the Kröger family? No, he didn't feel like it. And weren't these men of middle-class order basically a little bit right? In a way he quite agreed with them... He shrugged his shoulders and said nothing.
units.explain_en: Tonio could easily prove that he is the son of the town's respected Consul Kröger – but he doesn't, because deep down he feels the police are right to see him as an outsider. “der Hochstapler” = con man, impostor – still used. “sich zu erkennen geben” = to reveal who you are. “keine Lust haben” = not to feel like it: “Ich habe keine Lust!” Important: “Zigeuner” was the normal word in 1903, but today it is considered offensive – say “Sinti und Roma”. Tonio is repeating a phrase from Chapter I.

units.en: The policeman reads Tonio's proofs, and Herr Seehaase reads along. ‘Look – there's my name. I wrote this, and it's going to be published,’ says Tonio. That is good enough for Herr Seehaase, who sends the policeman, Petersen, away and sees his guest to the carriage with many apologies. So ends Tonio's strange stay in his home town. CHAPTER VII: At nightfall his steamer reaches the open sea. He felt a little low at nearly being arrested as a con man, but watching the ship being loaded – including a polar bear and a tiger in cages for a Danish zoo – cheered him up. Now, in the moonlight, he sees the distant beach where he spent his summers as a boy, the lighthouse and the lights of the spa hotel.

units.de: Die Ostsee! Er lehnte den Kopf gegen den starken Salzwind, der frei und ohne Hindernis daherkam, die Ohren umhüllte und einen gelinden Schwindel, eine gedämpfte Betäubung hervorrief, in der die Erinnerung an alles Böse, an Qual und Irrsal, an Wollen und Mühen träge und selig unterging. Und in dem Sausen, Klatschen, Schäumen und Ächzen rings um ihn her glaubte er das Rauschen und Knarren des alten Walnussbaumes, das Kreischen einer Gartenpforte zu hören... Es dunkelte mehr und mehr.
units.en: The Baltic! He leaned his head into the strong salt wind, which came freely and unhindered, wrapped itself around his ears and brought on a gentle dizziness, a muffled daze, in which the memory of everything bad, of torment and confusion, of wanting and struggling, sank away lazily and blissfully. And in the rushing, slapping, foaming and groaning all around him he thought he could hear the rustling and creaking of the old walnut tree and the squeaking of a garden gate... It grew darker and darker.
units.explain_en: For Tonio the sea means freedom and childhood. Mann piles up nouns made from verbs – “das Sausen, Klatschen, Schäumen und Ächzen” – so that we can hear the sea (any verb can become a neuter noun: “das Lesen”, “das Schwimmen”). “der Schwindel” = dizziness (and also a swindle!). “das Irrsal” is a rare old word for confusion. “Es dunkelte” is literary; today “Es wurde dunkel”. “mehr und mehr” = more and more (or “immer dunkler”).

units.en: On deck a young businessman from Hamburg, who ate an enormous amount of lobster omelette at dinner, gazes up at the sky. ‘Just look at the stars,’ he says, pronouncing it ‘Sderne’ in his Hamburg accent – next to them, we humans are nothing but worms. Tonio thinks with amusement that this man has no literature in him, and yet he feels friendly towards him. The man admits that he is often melancholy, and Tonio suspects he secretly writes poems. The wind gets stronger and they go to bed, but Tonio can't sleep and feels seasick, so he goes back on deck. A storm is raging: the waves leap up like flames, the polar bear and the tiger roar below deck, and the young man from Hamburg is being sick over the rail.

units.de: Tonio Kröger hielt sich an irgendeinem gestrafften Tau und blickte hinaus in all den unbändigen Übermut. In ihm schwang sich ein Jauchzen auf, und ihm war, als sei es mächtig genug, um Sturm und Flut zu übertönen. Ein Sang an das Meer, begeistert von Liebe, tönte in ihm. Du meiner Jugend wilder Freund, so sind wir einmal noch vereint... Aber dann war das Gedicht zu Ende. Es ward nicht fertig, nicht rund geformt und nicht in Gelassenheit zu etwas Ganzem geschmiedet. Sein Herz lebte...
units.en: Tonio Kröger held on to a taut rope and looked out into all that untamed wildness. A shout of joy rose up inside him, and it seemed to him mighty enough to drown out storm and sea. A song to the sea, inspired by love, sounded within him. You wild friend of my youth, so we are united once again... But then the poem was over. It didn't get finished, didn't get rounded off, wasn't calmly forged into a whole. His heart was alive...
units.explain_en: In Chapter II love stopped Tonio from shaping things calmly into a whole (“in Gelassenheit etwas Ganzes schmieden”). The same words return here: his poem doesn't get finished – and that's good news, because “sein Herz lebte” (his heart was alive) again, as when he was young. “ihm war, als sei es ...” = it seemed to him as if it were ... (Konjunktiv I). “übertönen” = to drown out (a sound). “ward” is old for “wurde”. “die Gelassenheit” = calmness – still used: “Bleib gelassen!” = Stay calm!

units.en: At dawn the ship passes the white chalk cliffs of Møn. Tonio spends three days sightseeing in Copenhagen, but what he really notices are familiar old names on the houses and, everywhere, blue eyes and blond hair like in his dreams. Restless, he travels on past Helsingør to a small white seaside hotel in Aalsgaard. CHAPTER VIII: It's September and there are few guests – the elderly landlady, a wheezing fish dealer from Copenhagen, and three silent American boys with their tutor. Tonio spends peaceful days on the beach and in the beech woods, forgetting time. Then one morning, after a glorious sunrise and a swim, he finds the hotel full of day-trippers from Helsingør. ‘There'll be a dance here tonight – we won't get a wink of sleep!’ grumbles the fish dealer.

units.de: Da geschah dies auf einmal: Hans Hansen und Ingeborg Holm gingen durch den Saal. – Tonio Kröger lehnte, in einer wohligen Ermüdung nach dem Bade und seinem hurtigen Gang, im Stuhl und aß geräucherten Lachs auf Röstbrot; – er saß der Veranda und dem Meere zugewandt. Und plötzlich öffnete sich die Tür, und Hand in Hand kamen die beiden herein, – schlendernd und ohne Eile.
units.en: Then, all of a sudden, this happened: Hans Hansen and Ingeborg Holm walked through the dining room. – Tonio Kröger was leaning back in his chair, pleasantly tired after his swim and his brisk walk, eating smoked salmon on toast; he was sitting facing the veranda and the sea. And suddenly the door opened, and the two of them came in hand in hand – strolling and in no hurry.
units.explain_en: The big surprise of the story. Mann states it as a plain fact – but read on carefully: are these really Hans and Inge from school, or a young Danish couple who look just like them? “auf einmal” = suddenly. “das Bad” here means the swim in the sea (“baden gehen” = to go swimming). “hurtig” is old-fashioned for “schnell”. “zugewandt” = facing (from “zuwenden”). “schlendern” = to stroll – still common.

words.note: Ich bin in Eile. = I'm in a hurry.

units.en: ‘Inge’ wears a light summer dress, just like at Herr Knaak's dance lessons, though her braid is now pinned up; ‘Hans’ wears his sailor jacket, swings his cap and stares defiantly at the people eating. (Mann never says whether they really are Hans and Inge or a Danish pair of exactly the same type.) The day-trippers drive off and come back in the evening for the dance. All day Tonio waits with an anxious, sweet joy he hasn't felt for years. When the music starts, he creeps down to the dark glass veranda and secretly watches the dancers through the open door. There they are: ‘Hans’ eating a big piece of cake near the door, ‘Inge’ resting by the wall. To Tonio they stand for everything light, cheerful and uncomplicated.

units.de: Er sah sie an, sah, wie Hans Hansen so keck und wohlgestaltet wie nur jemals, breit in den Schultern und schmal in den Hüften, in seinem Matrosenanzug dastand, sah, wie Ingeborg auf eine gewisse übermütige Art lachend den Kopf zur Seite warf, auf eine gewisse Art ihre Hand, eine gar nicht besonders schmale, gar nicht besonders feine Kleinmädchenhand, zum Hinterkopfe führte, wobei der leichte Ärmel von ihrem Ellenbogen zurückglitt, – und plötzlich erschütterte das Heimweh seine Brust mit einem solchen Schmerz, dass er unwillkürlich weiter ins Dunkel zurückwich, damit niemand das Zucken seines Gesichtes sähe.
units.en: He looked at them, saw how Hans Hansen stood there in his sailor suit, as bold and well-built as ever, broad in the shoulders and narrow in the hips; saw how Ingeborg tossed her head to one side, laughing in a certain high-spirited way, and in a certain way raised her hand – a not particularly slender, not particularly delicate little girl's hand – to the back of her head, so that the light sleeve slid back from her elbow – and suddenly homesickness shook his chest with such pain that he drew back further into the darkness without meaning to, so that no one would see his face twitch.
units.explain_en: These are almost the same words as the moment Tonio fell in love with Inge in Chapter II (“auf eine gewisse übermütige Art lachend den Kopf zur Seite warf ...”) – as if time had stood still. “das Heimweh” = homesickness (“Ich habe Heimweh”); here it is a longing for his lost youth, not just for a place. “unwillkürlich” = involuntarily, without meaning to. “damit niemand ... sähe” = so that no one would see (Konjunktiv II; today usually “sehen konnte”). “zucken” = to twitch.

units.de: Hatte ich euch vergessen? fragte er. Nein, niemals! Nicht dich, Hans, noch dich, blonde Inge! Ihr wart es ja, für die ich arbeitete, und wenn ich Applaus vernahm, blickte ich heimlich um mich, ob ihr daran teilhättet... Hast du nun den ›Don Carlos‹ gelesen, Hans Hansen, wie du es mir an eurer Gartenpforte versprachst? Tu's nicht! Ich verlange es nicht mehr von dir. Was geht dich der König an, der weint, weil er einsam ist? Du sollst deine hellen Augen nicht trüb und traumblöde machen vom Starren in Verse und Melancholie...
units.en: Had I forgotten you? he asked. No, never! Not you, Hans, nor you, blonde Inge! It was you I was working for, and whenever I heard applause I secretly looked around to see if you were part of it... Have you read ‘Don Carlos’ now, Hans Hansen, as you promised me at your garden gate? Don't! I don't ask it of you any more. What's the king who weeps because he is lonely to you? You shouldn't make your bright eyes dull and dreamy from staring at poems and melancholy...
units.explain_en: Tonio talks to them silently in his head, using “du” and “ihr” (plural you). In Chapter I Hans promised to read Schiller's play ‘Don Carlos’, about a lonely king – now Tonio doesn't want him to. “Tu's nicht!” = Don't (do it)! “Was geht dich ... an?” = What's ... to you? – very common: “Das geht dich nichts an!” = That's none of your business! “teilhaben an” = to share in. “verlangen” = to demand, ask for. “traumblöde” is Mann's own word: dazed from dreaming.

units.de: Zu sein wie du! Noch einmal anfangen, aufwachsen gleich dir, rechtschaffen, fröhlich und schlicht, regelrecht, ordnungsgemäß und im Einverständnis mit Gott und der Welt, geliebt werden von den Harmlosen und Glücklichen, dich zum Weibe nehmen, Ingeborg Holm, und einen Sohn haben wie du, Hans Hansen, – frei vom Fluch der Erkenntnis und der schöpferischen Qual leben, lieben und loben in seliger Gewöhnlichkeit!... Noch einmal anfangen? Aber es hülfe nichts. Es würde wieder so werden, – alles würde wieder so kommen, wie es gekommen ist. Denn etliche gehen mit Notwendigkeit in die Irre, weil es einen rechten Weg für sie überhaupt nicht gibt.
units.en: To be like you! To start again, to grow up like you, decent, cheerful and simple, normal, orderly and at peace with God and the world, loved by the harmless and happy, to take you as my wife, Ingeborg Holm, and to have a son like you, Hans Hansen – to live free from the curse of knowledge and the torment of creation, to live, love and praise in blissful ordinariness!... Start again? But it would be no use. It would all turn out the same – everything would happen again just the way it has happened. For some people go astray of necessity, because for them there simply is no right way.
units.explain_en: Tonio dreams of an ordinary life – then admits it would change nothing. The last sentence repeats the start of Chapter III. “jemanden zum Weibe nehmen” is very old: today “jemanden heiraten” (to marry someone); “das Weib” is old-fashioned and today sounds rude or insulting – say “die Frau”. “Es hülfe nichts” uses the old Konjunktiv II of “helfen”; today “Es würde nichts helfen” or “Das bringt nichts”. “mit Gott und der Welt” = with everybody. “in die Irre gehen” = to go astray.

sentences.de: Noch einmal anfangen, aufwachsen gleich dir, rechtschaffen, fröhlich und schlicht, regelrecht, ordnungsgemäß und im Einverständnis mit Gott und der Welt, geliebt werden von den Harmlosen und Glücklichen, dich zum Weibe nehmen, Ingeborg Holm, und einen Sohn haben wie du, Hans Hansen, – frei vom Fluch der Erkenntnis und der schöpferischen Qual leben, lieben und loben in seliger Gewöhnlichkeit!...

units.en: In the break ‘Hans’ and ‘Inge’ glance at Tonio with complete indifference. But a pale, thin girl whom hardly anyone has asked to dance keeps looking at him with dark, swimming eyes; he turns away. He longs to say something to Hans and Inge, just a joke to get a smile, but can't find the courage: their language is not his language. Then a quadrille begins, with French commands, just like at Herr Knaak's. Inge dances right in front of him, and he wonders whether she would still laugh at him now that he is famous – and thinks she'd be right to. In the wild final gallop the pale girl falls hard. Tonio helps her up. ‘Tak! O, mange Tak!’ (Danish: thank you so much), she says. ‘You shouldn't dance any more, Fräulein,’ he says gently, and leaves.

units.de: Er war berauscht von dem Feste, an dem er nicht teilgehabt, und müde von Eifersucht. Wie früher, ganz wie früher war es gewesen! Mit erhitztem Gesicht hatte er an dunkler Stelle gestanden, in Schmerzen um euch, ihr Blonden, Lebendigen, Glücklichen, und war dann einsam hinweggegangen. Jemand müsste nun kommen! Ingeborg müsste nun kommen, müsste bemerken, dass er fort war, müsste ihm heimlich folgen, ihm die Hand auf die Schulter legen und sagen: Komm herein zu uns! Sei froh! Ich liebe dich!...
units.en: He was intoxicated by the party he had not taken part in, and tired from jealousy. It had been like before, exactly like before! With a flushed face he had stood in a dark place, aching for you, you blond, living, happy ones, and had then gone away alone. Someone ought to come now! Ingeborg ought to come now, ought to notice that he had gone, ought to follow him secretly, put her hand on his shoulder and say: Come in and join us! Be happy! I love you!...
units.explain_en: This is the same wish Tonio had at sixteen, in the corridor after the dance lesson, almost word for word – the story comes full circle. “berauscht” = intoxicated (“der Rausch” = intoxication, high). “die Eifersucht” = jealousy; “eifersüchtig” = jealous. “müsste” (Konjunktiv II of “müssen”) = ought to: “Sie müsste eigentlich gleich kommen.” “an dem er nicht teilgehabt” – Mann leaves out the “hatte” at the end, which is old-fashioned.

units.de: Aber sie kam keines Weges. Dergleichen geschah nicht. Ja, wie damals war es, und er war glücklich wie damals. Denn sein Herz lebte. Was aber war gewesen während all der Zeit, in der er das geworden, was er nun war? – Erstarrung; Öde; Eis; und Geist! Und Kunst!... Er entkleidete sich, legte sich zur Ruhe, löschte das Licht. Er flüsterte zwei Namen in das Kissen hinein, diese paar keuschen, nordischen Silben, die ihm seine eigentliche und ursprüngliche Liebes-, Leides- und Glückesart, das Leben, das simple und innige Gefühl, die Heimat bezeichneten. Er blickte zurück auf die Jahre seit damals bis auf diesen Tag.
units.en: But she did not come at all. Things like that didn't happen. Yes, it was just like back then, and he was happy, as he had been back then. For his heart was alive. But what had there been during all the time in which he had become what he now was? – Numbness; emptiness; ice; and intellect! And art!... He undressed, lay down to rest and put out the light. He whispered two names into the pillow, those few chaste, northern syllables that stood for his true and original way of loving, suffering and being happy, for life, for simple and heartfelt feeling, for home. He looked back over the years from then until this day.
units.explain_en: “Denn sein Herz lebte” – the key sentence from Chapters I and II returns: feeling lonely and hurt means his heart is alive again, after years of “Eis” (ice) and “Geist” (intellect). “keines Weges” is Mann's spelling of “keineswegs” (not at all). “Dergleichen” = things like that (formal; everyday “so was”). “das Licht löschen” = to put out the light (everyday “das Licht ausmachen”). “die Heimat” = home, homeland – a word full of feeling in German.

units.de: Er gedachte der wüsten Abenteuer der Sinne, der Nerven und des Gedankens, die er durchlebt, sah sich zerfressen von Ironie und Geist, verödet und gelähmt von Erkenntnis, halb aufgerieben von den Fiebern und Frösten des Schaffens, haltlos und unter Gewissensnöten zwischen krassen Extremen, zwischen Heiligkeit und Brunst hin und her geworfen, raffiniert, verarmt, erschöpft von kalten und künstlich erlesenen Exaltationen, verirrt, verwüstet, zermartert, krank – und schluchzte vor Reue und Heimweh. Um ihn war es still und dunkel. Aber von unten tönte gedämpft und wiegend des Lebens süßer, trivialer Dreitakt zu ihm herauf.
units.en: He thought of the wild adventures of the senses, the nerves and the mind that he had lived through, saw himself eaten away by irony and intellect, laid waste and paralysed by knowledge, half worn out by the fevers and chills of creating, tossed back and forth, unsteady and tormented by his conscience, between crude extremes, between holiness and lust – over-refined, impoverished, exhausted by cold and artificial raptures, lost, ruined, tortured, sick – and he sobbed with remorse and homesickness. Around him all was quiet and dark. But from below, muffled and swaying, the sweet, trivial three-four time of life drifted up to him.
units.explain_en: CHAPTER VIII ends. The long sentence lists everything that went wrong in Tonio's adult life, until it breaks off in sobbing. “gedenken” (+ genitive) is old-fashioned for “denken an”. “die Brunst” is a strong old word for animal lust. “schluchzen” = to sob. “die Reue” = remorse, regret (“bereuen” = to regret). The “Dreitakt” is the waltz rhythm of the dance downstairs: ordinary life goes on, sweet and a bit banal – without him.

units.de: Tonio Kröger saß im Norden und schrieb an Lisaweta Iwanowna, seine Freundin, wie er es ihr versprochen hatte. Liebe Lisaweta dort unten in Arkadien, wohin ich bald zurückkehren werde, schrieb er. Hier ist nun also so etwas wie ein Brief, aber er wird Sie wohl enttäuschen, denn ich denke, ihn ein wenig allgemein zu halten. Nicht, dass ich so gar nichts zu erzählen, auf meine Weise nicht dies und das erlebt hätte. Zu Hause, in meiner Vaterstadt, wollte man mich sogar verhaften... aber davon sollen Sie mündlich hören. Ich habe jetzt manchmal Tage, an denen ich es vorziehe, auf gute Art etwas Allgemeines zu sagen, anstatt Geschichten zu erzählen.
units.en: Tonio Kröger sat in the North and wrote to Lisaweta Ivanovna, his friend, as he had promised her. Dear Lisaweta down there in Arcadia, where I shall soon return, he wrote. So here is something like a letter, but it will probably disappoint you, because I intend to keep it rather general. Not that I have nothing at all to tell, or haven't experienced this and that in my own way. At home, in my native town, they even wanted to arrest me... but you shall hear about that in person. These days I sometimes have days when I prefer to say something general in a good way rather than tell stories.
units.explain_en: CHAPTER IX, the last, is Tonio's letter to Lisaweta – the one she asked for at the end of Chapter V. “Arkadien” (Arcadia) is the ancient Greek dreamland of happy shepherds; Tonio jokingly means sunny Munich. “verhaften” = to arrest – still the normal word. “mündlich” = in person, spoken (the opposite of “schriftlich”, in writing). “etwas vorziehen” = to prefer something: “Ich ziehe Tee vor.” “Nicht, dass ...” = not that ...

units.de: Wissen Sie wohl noch, Lisaweta, dass Sie mich einmal einen Bürger, einen verirrten Bürger nannten? Sie nannten mich so in einer Stunde, da ich Ihnen, verführt durch andere Geständnisse, die ich mir vorher hatte entschlüpfen lassen, meine Liebe zu dem gestand, was ich das ›Leben‹ nenne; und ich frage mich, ob Sie wohl wussten, wie sehr Sie damit die Wahrheit trafen, wie sehr mein Bürgertum und meine Liebe zum ›Leben‹ eins und dasselbe sind. Diese Reise hat mir Veranlassung gegeben, darüber nachzudenken...
units.en: Do you still remember, Lisaweta, that you once called me a bourgeois, a bourgeois gone astray? You called me that at a moment when, carried away by other confessions I had let slip before, I confessed to you my love for what I call ‘life’; and I wonder whether you knew how very much you hit the truth, how very much my bourgeois nature and my love of ‘life’ are one and the same. This journey has given me cause to think about it...
units.explain_en: Tonio now agrees with Lisaweta's verdict from Chapter IV and explains it. “Wissen Sie wohl noch ...?” = Do you still remember ...? (today “Erinnern Sie sich noch ...?” or, among friends, “Weißt du noch ...?”). “in einer Stunde, da ...” – “da” here means “when” (old-fashioned; today “als”). “entschlüpfen” = to slip out. “die Wahrheit treffen” = to hit the truth. “eins und dasselbe” = one and the same. “die Veranlassung” = reason, occasion (today usually “der Anlass”).

units.de: Mein Vater, wissen Sie, war ein nordisches Temperament: betrachtsam, gründlich, korrekt aus Puritanismus und zur Wehmut geneigt; meine Mutter von unbestimmt exotischem Blut, schön, sinnlich, naiv, zugleich fahrlässig und leidenschaftlich und von einer impulsiven Liederlichkeit. Ganz ohne Zweifel war dies eine Mischung, die außerordentliche Möglichkeiten – und außerordentliche Gefahren in sich schloss.
units.en: My father, you know, had a northern temperament: thoughtful, thorough, correct out of Puritanism and inclined to melancholy; my mother was of vaguely exotic blood, beautiful, sensual, naive, both careless and passionate, and impulsively disorderly. Without any doubt this was a mixture that held extraordinary possibilities – and extraordinary dangers.
units.explain_en: Tonio explains himself through his parents: the serious northern father and the passionate southern mother. Explaining someone's character by their “Blut” (blood) was common around 1900, but today it sounds like old racial thinking – we would talk about background or upbringing. “geneigt zu” = inclined to. “die Liederlichkeit” = sloppiness, loose living (old-fashioned). “Ganz ohne Zweifel” = without any doubt – still normal.

units.de: Was herauskam, war dies: ein Bürger, der sich in die Kunst verirrte, ein Bohemien mit Heimweh nach der guten Kinderstube, ein Künstler mit schlechtem Gewissen. Denn mein bürgerliches Gewissen ist es ja, was mich in allem Künstlertum, aller Außerordentlichkeit und allem Genie etwas tief Zweideutiges, tief Anrüchiges, tief Zweifelhaftes erblicken lässt, was mich mit dieser verliebten Schwäche für das Simple, Treuherzige und Angenehm-Normale, das Ungeniale und Anständige erfüllt.
units.en: What came out of it was this: a bourgeois who strayed into art, a bohemian homesick for a good upbringing, an artist with a bad conscience. For it is my bourgeois conscience that makes me see something deeply ambiguous, deeply disreputable, deeply dubious in all artistry, all extraordinariness and all genius, and that fills me with this lovesick weakness for the simple, the true-hearted and the pleasantly normal, for what is decent and not a genius.
units.explain_en: The famous self-description: “ein Künstler mit schlechtem Gewissen” – an artist with a bad conscience. “Was herauskam, war dies” = what came out of it was this (“Was ist dabei herausgekommen?” = What was the result?). “ein Bohemien” = a free-living artist type. “ein schlechtes Gewissen haben” = to feel guilty – very common. “zweideutig” = ambiguous (literally “two-meaning”); “anrüchig” = shady, disreputable. “eine Schwäche für” = a soft spot for: “Ich habe eine Schwäche für Schokolade.”

units.de: Ich stehe zwischen zwei Welten, bin in keiner daheim und habe es infolgedessen ein wenig schwer. Ihr Künstler nennt mich einen Bürger, und die Bürger sind versucht, mich zu verhaften... ich weiß nicht, was von beiden mich bitterer kränkt. Die Bürger sind dumm; ihr Anbeter der Schönheit aber, die ihr mich phlegmatisch und ohne Sehnsucht heißt, solltet bedenken, dass es ein Künstlertum gibt, so tief, so von Anbeginn und Schicksals wegen, dass keine Sehnsucht ihm süßer und empfindenswerter erscheint als die nach den Wonnen der Gewöhnlichkeit.
units.en: I stand between two worlds, I am at home in neither, and so I have rather a hard time of it. You artists call me a bourgeois, and the bourgeois are tempted to arrest me... I don't know which of the two hurts me more bitterly. The bourgeois are stupid; but you worshippers of beauty, who call me dull and without longing, should remember that there is a kind of artistry so deep, so much there from the very beginning and by fate, that no longing seems sweeter and more worth feeling to it than the longing for the joys of the ordinary.
units.explain_en: “Ich stehe zwischen zwei Welten, bin in keiner daheim” is one of Thomas Mann's most quoted sentences – many people who grow up between two cultures recognise themselves in it. “es schwer haben” = to have a hard time: “Er hat es nicht leicht.” “versucht sein” = to be tempted. “kränken” = to hurt someone's feelings. “heißen” here is old-fashioned for “nennen” (to call someone something). “phlegmatisch” = sluggish, unemotional. “daheim” = at home (southern German; elsewhere “zu Hause”).

units.de: Ich bewundere die Stolzen und Kalten, die auf den Pfaden der großen, der dämonischen Schönheit abenteuern und den ›Menschen‹ verachten, – aber ich beneide sie nicht. Denn wenn irgendetwas imstande ist, aus einem Literaten einen Dichter zu machen, so ist es diese meine Bürgerliebe zum Menschlichen, Lebendigen und Gewöhnlichen. Alle Wärme, alle Güte, aller Humor kommt aus ihr, und fast will mir scheinen, als sei sie jene Liebe selbst, von der geschrieben steht, dass einer mit Menschen- und Engelszungen reden könne und ohne sie doch nur ein tönendes Erz und eine klingende Schelle sei.
units.en: I admire the proud and cold who go adventuring on the paths of great, demonic beauty and despise ‘human beings’ – but I don't envy them. For if anything can make a poet out of a mere man of letters, it is this bourgeois love of mine for the human, the living and the ordinary. All warmth, all kindness, all humour come from it, and it almost seems to me as if it were that very love of which it is written that a man may speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and without it still be only a sounding brass and a tinkling cymbal.
units.explain_en: The end of this passage quotes the Bible (1 Corinthians 13): “Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not love, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal.” Tonio separates a “Literat” (a clever writer) from a “Dichter” (a true poet): what makes the difference is love for ordinary people. “bewundern” = to admire; “beneiden” = to envy. “imstande sein” = to be able to (formal; everyday “können”). “fast will mir scheinen” = it almost seems to me (old-fashioned; today “Mir scheint fast”).

sentences.de: Ich bewundere die Stolzen und Kalten, die auf den Pfaden der großen, der dämonischen Schönheit abenteuern und den ›Menschen‹ verachten, – aber ich beneide sie nicht.
sentences.en: I admire the proud and cold who go adventuring on the paths of great, demonic beauty and despise ‘human beings’ – but I don't envy them.

sentences.de: Denn wenn irgendetwas imstande ist, aus einem Literaten einen Dichter zu machen, so ist es diese meine Bürgerliebe zum Menschlichen, Lebendigen und Gewöhnlichen.
sentences.en: For if anything can make a poet out of a mere man of letters, it is this bourgeois love of mine for the human, the living and the ordinary.

sentences.de: Alle Wärme, alle Güte, aller Humor kommt aus ihr, und fast will mir scheinen, als sei sie jene Liebe selbst, von der geschrieben steht, dass einer mit Menschen- und Engelszungen reden könne und ohne sie doch nur ein tönendes Erz und eine klingende Schelle sei.
sentences.en: All warmth, all kindness, all humour come from it, and it almost seems to me as if it were that very love of which it is written that a man may speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and without it still be only a sounding brass and a tinkling cymbal.

units.de: Was ich getan habe, ist nichts, nicht viel, so gut wie nichts. Ich werde Besseres machen, Lisaweta, – dies ist ein Versprechen. Während ich schreibe, rauscht das Meer zu mir herauf, und ich schließe die Augen. Ich schaue in eine ungeborene und schemenhafte Welt hinein, die geordnet und gebildet sein will, ich sehe in ein Gewimmel von Schatten menschlicher Gestalten, die mir winken, dass ich sie banne und erlöse: tragische und lächerliche und solche, die beides zugleich sind, – und diesen bin ich sehr zugetan.
units.en: What I have done is nothing, not much, as good as nothing. I will do better things, Lisaweta – this is a promise. As I write, the sea murmurs up to me, and I close my eyes. I look into an unborn, shadowy world that wants to be ordered and shaped; I see a swarm of shadowy human figures who beckon to me to capture them and set them free: tragic ones and ridiculous ones and ones that are both at once – and I am very fond of those.
units.explain_en: Tonio feels his next books coming: characters are waiting to be written. “so gut wie nichts” = as good as nothing – very common. “das Versprechen” = promise (a verb used as a noun). “das Gewimmel” = swarm, throng (“Es wimmelt von Ameisen” = It's teeming with ants). “winken” = to wave, to beckon. “bannen” = to capture (as if by magic); “erlösen” = to set free, to redeem. “jemandem zugetan sein” is old-fashioned for “jemanden mögen”.

units.de: Aber meine tiefste und verstohlenste Liebe gehört den Blonden und Blauäugigen, den hellen Lebendigen, den Glücklichen, Liebenswürdigen und Gewöhnlichen. Schelten Sie diese Liebe nicht, Lisaweta; sie ist gut und fruchtbar. Sehnsucht ist darin und schwermütiger Neid und ein klein wenig Verachtung und eine ganze keusche Seligkeit.
units.en: But my deepest and most secret love belongs to the blond and blue-eyed, the bright and living, the happy, the lovable and the ordinary. Don't scold this love, Lisaweta; it is good and fruitful. There is longing in it, and gloomy envy, and just a little contempt, and a whole, innocent bliss.
units.explain_en: THE END. The very last sentence repeats the last sentence of Chapter I almost word for word – “war darin” (was in it) has become “ist darin” (is in it): Tonio's heart is still alive. In the story “die Blonden und Blauäugigen” stand for people like Hans and Inge – cheerful, uncomplicated, “normal” people – not for a race (although ideas like this were later misused in terrible ways). “schelten” (schalt, hat gescholten) is old-fashioned for “schimpfen”. “fruchtbar” = fruitful.
